concept.name: Maximum position limit
concept.definition: A cap on the size of the net long or net short position a single person or account may hold or control in a given instrument, set by regulators or exchanges (speculative position limits) and by firms internally, to curb concentration and market-cornering risk.
concept.intuition: No single player should be big enough to break the market or break themselves; the limit predetermines how much is too much.
concept.mechanics: U.S. federal speculative position limits (17 CFR Part 150) cap spot-month and non-spot-month positions in referenced commodity contracts on a futures-equivalent basis, with exemptions for bona fide hedging; positions under common ownership (10%+) or control are aggregated. Exchanges set their own limits or accountability levels, and crypto venues implement analogous tiered caps on position value per leverage tier.
concept.formula: Constraint: |net futures-equivalent position| <= limit for the contract and month; aggregation sums positions across all accounts with 10 percent or greater ownership or common trading control.
concept.failure_modes: Limits bind only within one venue or regime: exposure can be rebuilt in exempted instruments, offshore venues, or economically equivalent swaps before anti-evasion rules catch up. They also do nothing about many sub-limit positions correlating in a crisis.
concept.misconceptions: Position limits are not margin requirements — one caps quantity, the other prices collateral — and the visible cap is not the whole story, since bona fide hedgers and certain entities receive exemptions.
concept.example: Under 17 CFR 150.2, no person may hold or control spot-month positions in a core referenced futures contract above the Commission-set level, net long or net short, absent an exemption such as a bona fide hedge.

citations.source: eCFR: 17 CFR Part 150 — Limits on Positions
citations.section: 150.1 (definition of speculative position limit); 150.2 (Federal speculative position limits)
